newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina stages painful homage to Jewish attack.
newsitem.headline: Argentina stages painful homage to Jewish attack.

text.p: Argentina marked the fifth anniversary of the bombing of the Israeli Embassy in Buenos Aires on Monday with mourning and angry attacks on authorities for failing to find the culprits.

The leader of Argentina's Jewish community, Ruben Beraja, criticised the government and the Supreme Court for not committing to investigating the explosion that killed 29 people and injured more than 200 on March 17, 1992.

"It was investigated as though it were just another crime," said Beraja, president of the DAIA umbrella of Jewish groups in Argentina. "This crime was more horrid, more treacherous and with more victims but there was no strategic plan to analyse who could have been behind it.
"The Supreme Court, by the way it went about the case, revealed it was not prepared for an investigation of this kind," he said.
The attack was followed by an even bloodier car bomb attack at the AMIA Jewish community centre that killed 86 and injured hundreds in 1994. Both cases remain unsolved.
Argentine police have been regularly criticised by the Jewish community, one of the largest in the world, by Israel and by the United States for their slow progress investigating both attacks.

As Jewish schoolchildren across Argentina held memorials in their classrooms, cabinet ministers, victims' relatives and other members of the Jewish community held a moment of silence and read the names of the dead at the Tablada Jewish cemetery just outside Buenos Aires.
Israel's Ambassador to Argentina, Itzhak Aviran, accused the high court of "burying the case in a drawer." Israel has blamed the embassy bombing on Iranian-backed fundamentalists.
"We are orphans (of justice)," Aviran said. "We know that when one looks for the truth one finds it.
"Every country must safeguard each one of its citizens and its guests," he said. "A diplomatic mission is a guest in the country. I say it painfully. It was not sufficiently looked after."
Argentine officials insisted they would continue to pursue those responsible for both attacks on the Jewish community.
"We are firmly convinced that no matter how much time has passed, the will to clear this up continues and is firm," Argentine Interior Minister Carlos Corach told reporters.
"I don't think this will remain unpunished," Justice Minister Elias Jassan added.
Israeli police head Asaf Hefetz travelled to Buenos Aires last month to monitor investigations into the bombings.

"The most important thing is not to forget," Jorge Cohen, a former embassy press secretary who survived the blast, told Reuters. "One begins to forget because you can't carry the tragedy around with you all the time. One tries to continue on in life the best way possible."
